Rule_Name: Memory Demand Must Be Characterized by Workload Execution Context
Rule_Description: Before comparing a workload with hardware memory, DSS must identify the execution mode and memory-relevant workload context, including model/parameter representation, numerical precision, training versus fine-tuning versus inference, batch/concurrency and sequence/context characteristics when applicable. A universal memory requirement must not be assumed.
Inputs: Workload execution mode; model parameter count/representation; numerical precision; batch size; concurrency; sequence/context length; runtime memory-management technique
Condition: Memory demand is evaluated without a defined workload execution context
Output_Decision: INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE until the applicable workload context is specified
Source_Title: ZeRO; Training Deep Nets with Sublinear Memory Cost; PagedAttention; QLoRA
Exact_Page_Section_Table_Equation: ZeRO: memory-consumption discussion and model-state/residual-state analysis; Sublinear Memory: Abstract and Introduction; PagedAttention: Abstract and memory-management discussion; QLoRA: §3 QLoRA Finetuning
Evidence: The papers show memory demand depends on model states, activations, sequence/context behavior, quantization and serving cache behavior rather than one universal workload constant.
Applicability: All AI workloads evaluated for memory feasibility.
Limitations: The required workload variables differ by model family and runtime; not every variable applies to every workload.

Rule_Name: Host and Accelerator Memory Must Be Treated as Distinct Capacity Pools
Rule_Description: DSS must distinguish host/system memory from GPU/accelerator memory when evaluating capacity. A workload requiring accelerator-resident data cannot be declared feasible solely because the server has sufficient host memory.
Inputs: System_Memory_GB; GPU_Memory_Per_Accelerator_GB; GPU_Memory_Aggregate_GB; workload memory placement
Condition: Required memory is assigned to one memory pool but feasibility is evaluated using a different pool
Output_Decision: INFEASIBLE for that placement, or INSufficient Evidence if placement is unspecified
Source_Title: Part 0 Memory Catalogue Audit; QLoRA; ZeRO
Exact_Page_Section_Table_Equation: Part 0 Field Register; QLoRA §3; ZeRO model-state/residual-state memory analysis
Evidence: QLoRA explicitly uses GPU memory and CPU memory through paged optimizers; ZeRO analyzes device memory for model states and residual states. These distinguish memory locations rather than treating system RAM and accelerator memory as interchangeable.
Applicability: Single-node and distributed workloads with explicit memory placement.
Limitations: Some runtimes support managed/offloaded memory; such mechanisms must be explicitly specified rather than assumed.

Rule_Name: Configured Host Memory Must Be Used for Current Capacity Feasibility
Rule_Description: For a current server configuration, DSS should evaluate host-memory feasibility using the configured/installed system-memory value represented by System_Memory_GB. Memory_Max_GB represents a supported maximum/configuration envelope and must not be treated as currently installed memory unless the configuration explicitly establishes it.
Inputs: System_Memory_GB; System_Memory_Status; Memory_Max_GB; Memory_Max_Status
Condition: Current configured host-memory feasibility is evaluated using maximum supported memory instead of configured memory
Output_Decision: Use System_Memory_GB for current capacity; use Memory_Max_GB only for supported-capacity/configuration analysis
Source_Title: AI SERVER(6).CSV; Dell PowerEdge XE9680 Memory Specifications; HPE ProLiant DL380 Gen11 QuickSpecs
Exact_Page_Section_Table_Equation: Dell: Memory specifications Tables 1–3; HPE: QuickSpecs Memory section
Evidence: Vendor documentation distinguishes configured memory population/capacity from maximum supported capacity and documents model-specific population constraints.
Applicability: Current server configuration selection and upgrade feasibility.
Limitations: The catalogue's System_Memory_Status includes mixed VERIFIED/ESTIMATED evidence, so status must be retained.

Rule_Name: Single-Accelerator Workloads Must Be Checked Against Per-Accelerator Memory
Rule_Description: When the workload must fit on one accelerator, DSS must compare its applicable accelerator-memory demand against GPU_Memory_Per_Accelerator_GB rather than GPU_Memory_Aggregate_GB.
Inputs: GPU_Memory_Per_Accelerator_GB; GPU_Memory_Per_Accelerator_Status; workload applicable accelerator-memory demand
Condition: Workload placement requires a single accelerator and demand exceeds that accelerator's available memory
Output_Decision: INFEASIBLE on the candidate accelerator
Source_Title: GPU catalogue audit; NVIDIA H200 GPU; AMD Instinct MI300X Accelerator
Exact_Page_Section_Table_Equation: NVIDIA H200 Specifications; AMD MI300X Specifications table
Evidence: Vendor specifications explicitly state memory capacity per physical accelerator, while the project GPU catalogue separately records per-accelerator and aggregate memory.
Applicability: Single-GPU execution and any placement requiring all applicable model state to reside on one accelerator.
Limitations: Does not determine whether distributed sharding/offload can make a workload feasible.

Rule_Name: Aggregate GPU Memory Must Not Be Treated as One Shared Pool Without a Supported Distribution Strategy
Rule_Description: DSS may use GPU_Memory_Aggregate_GB only when the workload/runtime explicitly supports a distribution strategy that maps the required model state or workload memory across the participating accelerators.
Inputs: GPU_Memory_Aggregate_GB; GPU_Memory_Per_Accelerator_GB; workload parallel/distribution strategy
Condition: Aggregate GPU memory is used for feasibility while no model/data/pipeline/sharding strategy establishes how memory is distributed
Output_Decision: INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE; do not treat aggregate memory as automatically usable
Source_Title: Part 0 Memory Catalogue Audit; ZeRO; Megatron-LM
Exact_Page_Section_Table_Equation: ZeRO: model-state partitioning analysis; Megatron-LM: model-parallelism method and memory-constraint discussion
Evidence: ZeRO partitions model states across devices; Megatron-LM uses model parallelism to overcome per-device memory constraints. Therefore aggregate capacity becomes relevant only through an explicit distribution mechanism.
Applicability: Multi-GPU training/fine-tuning and distributed inference when model-state distribution is supported.
Limitations: The rule does not prescribe a specific parallelism strategy or claim linear usable capacity.

Rule_Name: Training Feasibility Must Account for Model States Beyond Parameters
Rule_Description: For training, DSS must account for the memory components required by the selected training method, including parameters, gradients, optimizer states and activations/residual runtime state where applicable. Parameter memory alone is insufficient to establish training feasibility.
Inputs: Training method; parameter representation; gradients; optimizer state; activation/runtime memory requirements; applicable accelerator/host memory
Condition: Training feasibility is declared using parameter/weight memory alone
Output_Decision: INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE until applicable training memory components are accounted for
Source_Title: ZeRO: Memory Optimizations Toward Training Trillion Parameter Models; Training Deep Nets with Sublinear Memory Cost
Exact_Page_Section_Table_Equation: ZeRO: model-state and residual-state memory analysis; Sublinear Memory: §1 Introduction and memory-cost analysis
Evidence: ZeRO identifies optimizer states, gradients and parameters as major model-state memory and activations, temporary buffers and fragmentation as residual state. Chen et al. focus on intermediate feature maps and gradients as important training memory costs.
Applicability: Full training and any fine-tuning method that materializes gradients/optimizer state.
Limitations: Exact component sizes depend on optimizer, precision, architecture, batch/sequence characteristics and framework; no universal multiplier is used.

Rule_Name: Activation Memory Must Be Evaluated in the Context of the Training Workload
Rule_Description: If activations/intermediate feature maps materially contribute to training memory, DSS must evaluate them using the actual model/workload context rather than applying a fixed activation percentage or multiplier.
Inputs: Model architecture; depth/layer structure; sequence/unrolling length; batch size; activation precision; training memory-management method
Condition: Activation memory is represented by a universal fixed percentage/multiplier independent of workload context
Output_Decision: Use context-specific activation evidence or mark INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE
Source_Title: Training Deep Nets with Sublinear Memory Cost
Exact_Page_Section_Table_Equation: §1 Introduction; memory-cost analysis; experiments on feature-map memory
Evidence: The paper shows intermediate feature-map memory varies with network/workload structure and can be reduced by computation-for-memory tradeoffs. Its results are model/task specific and therefore do not support a universal activation multiplier.
Applicability: Training workloads with material activation/intermediate-state memory.
Limitations: Does not provide a universal activation-memory formula for arbitrary models.

Rule_Name: Activation-Recomputation or Checkpointing Changes the Applicable Training Memory Requirement
Rule_Description: If the selected training configuration uses activation recomputation/checkpointing, DSS must evaluate the resulting memory requirement under that configuration rather than using the unoptimized activation footprint.
Inputs: Training configuration; activation-recomputation/checkpointing setting; workload activation demand
Condition: Activation-recomputation/checkpointing is enabled but memory feasibility uses an unmodified activation footprint
Output_Decision: Recompute the applicable memory requirement under the selected method or return INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE
Source_Title: Training Deep Nets with Sublinear Memory Cost; QLoRA
Exact_Page_Section_Table_Equation: Sublinear Memory §4–§5; QLoRA §3 QLoRA Finetuning
Evidence: Both works use memory-saving techniques that trade computation or paging for reduced peak memory. Therefore the selected memory-management configuration affects the applicable capacity requirement.
Applicability: Training/fine-tuning systems using recomputation/checkpointing or related memory-saving methods.
Limitations: No universal reduction factor is assumed.

Rule_Name: Quantized Fine-Tuning Must Use the Selected Representation and Trainable-State Configuration
Rule_Description: For quantized/parameter-efficient fine-tuning, DSS must evaluate memory using the actual weight representation and trainable-state configuration. A full-precision full-training memory model must not be reused unchanged.
Inputs: Weight precision/quantization; frozen base-model status; trainable adapter parameters; optimizer configuration; applicable memory pools
Condition: Quantized/parameter-efficient fine-tuning is selected but full-precision full-parameter training memory is assumed
Output_Decision: Use configuration-specific memory accounting
Source_Title: QLoRA: Efficient Finetuning of Quantized LLMs
Exact_Page_Section_Table_Equation: §3 QLoRA Finetuning; 4-bit NormalFloat Quantization; Paged Optimizers
Evidence: QLoRA stores the base model in a low-precision representation while training low-rank adapters and uses paged optimizers to manage memory spikes. Its configuration is therefore materially different from full-parameter full-precision training.
Applicability: QLoRA-like or other explicitly quantized/parameter-efficient fine-tuning configurations.
Limitations: QLoRA's reported model sizes and hardware are study-specific and are not universal thresholds.

Rule_Name: Inference Feasibility Must Include Runtime State in Addition to Model Weights
Rule_Description: For inference, DSS must not evaluate memory using model/weight storage alone. The applicable runtime must account for activation/runtime state and, for autoregressive attention workloads where used, KV-cache memory.
Inputs: Model/weight representation; inference runtime; activation/runtime memory; KV-cache requirement where applicable; batch/concurrency/context length
Condition: Inference capacity is declared from weight memory alone while runtime state can consume additional memory
Output_Decision: INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE until applicable runtime memory is accounted for
Source_Title: Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention
Exact_Page_Section_Table_Equation: Abstract; §2 background/memory-management discussion
Evidence: PagedAttention identifies KV-cache memory per request as large, dynamic and capable of limiting batch size; memory fragmentation and duplication can waste available GPU memory.
Applicability: Autoregressive LLM/VLM serving and other inference systems using attention state that persists across decoding steps.
Limitations: KV cache is not applicable to every model or inference architecture.

Rule_Name: KV-Cache Demand Must Be Evaluated Against Active Serving Context
Rule_Description: When KV caching is used, DSS must treat KV-cache demand as dependent on active requests and context/sequence behavior rather than as a fixed memory constant.
Inputs: KV-cache enabled/disabled; active request count/concurrency; context/sequence length; model attention configuration; cache management method
Condition: KV-cache capacity is represented by a fixed constant independent of active serving context
Output_Decision: Evaluate KV-cache demand for the selected serving context or return INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE
Source_Title: Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention
Exact_Page_Section_Table_Equation: Abstract; memory-management discussion on dynamic KV cache and batching
Evidence: The paper states that KV cache for each request grows/shrinks dynamically and that batching and memory fragmentation affect usable memory.
Applicability: LLM serving with KV caching.
Limitations: The rule does not impose a fixed KV-cache multiplier; exact demand is runtime/model dependent.

Rule_Name: Replicated Memory Requires Per-Device Feasibility
Rule_Description: When a distributed workload replicates the relevant model state on each device, DSS must check the applicable memory demand against each participating device rather than treating aggregate device memory as one pool.
Inputs: Distribution strategy; per-device GPU memory; per-device applicable model state
Condition: Relevant model state is replicated and any participating device cannot hold its applicable replicated state
Output_Decision: INFEASIBLE under the selected replicated placement
Source_Title: ZeRO; Memory Catalogue Audit
Exact_Page_Section_Table_Equation: ZeRO: data-parallel baseline and model-state partitioning discussion
Evidence: ZeRO motivates partitioning because conventional data/model parallel approaches can duplicate state across devices. The applicable memory requirement therefore depends on whether state is replicated or partitioned.
Applicability: Distributed training/fine-tuning configurations with replicated state.
Limitations: Exact memory allocation depends on the selected distributed framework and strategy.

Rule_Name: Sharded Memory Requires a Verified Mapping of Model State Across Devices
Rule_Description: When memory is sharded/partitioned across devices, DSS may use the distributed capacity only after the selected sharding strategy establishes which model states are placed on each device and the resulting per-device memory requirements are satisfied.
Inputs: Sharding/parallelism strategy; GPU_Memory_Per_Accelerator_GB; model-state placement; applicable per-device memory demand
Condition: Sharded execution is claimed but per-device state placement and capacity have not been established
Output_Decision: INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE; do not assume aggregate memory is fully usable
Source_Title: ZeRO; Megatron-LM; Memory Catalogue Audit
Exact_Page_Section_Table_Equation: ZeRO model-state partitioning analysis; Megatron-LM model-parallel method
Evidence: ZeRO explicitly partitions optimizer states, gradients and parameters across data-parallel devices in different stages; Megatron-LM uses intra-layer model parallelism to distribute model computation/state.
Applicability: Distributed training/fine-tuning and model-parallel execution.
Limitations: No universal linear scaling or fixed per-device partition factor is assumed.

Rule_Name: Memory Feasibility Must Compare Required Applicable Memory With Available Applicable Memory
Rule_Description: A candidate configuration is memory-feasible only when the workload's required memory for the selected execution mode and placement is no greater than the applicable available memory pool at the relevant granularity (per accelerator, per host, or distributed per-device allocation).
Inputs: Required applicable memory; available applicable memory; execution mode; placement/distribution strategy
Input_Source: Derived DSS integration logic grounded in Part 0 catalogue fields and research evidence
Condition: Required applicable memory is greater than available applicable memory
Output_Decision: INFEASIBLE; otherwise FEASIBLE if all required placement/configuration conditions are satisfied
Source_Type: Derived DSS Rule + Catalogue + Research + Official Vendor
Source_Title: Part 0 Memory Catalogue Audit; ZeRO; PagedAttention; Dell XE9680; NVIDIA H200; AMD MI300X
Organisation: DSS Project; research literature; Dell; NVIDIA; AMD
Exact_Page_Section_Table_Equation: Derived DSS gate; supported by vendor memory-capacity specifications and research memory-placement analyses
Evidence: This is the fundamental capacity decision condition, but the operands are explicitly defined by execution mode and memory placement; research and vendor evidence show that capacity is device/pool/configuration specific.
Applicability: All Part 1 memory-capacity decisions.
Limitations: The formula does not estimate workload memory demand; later workload/memory methods must supply the required-memory operand. It does not assume aggregate memory is shared.

Rule_Name: Training Memory Must Include All Applicable Model-State and Residual Components
Rule_Description: For a training configuration, DSS must identify the applicable parameters, gradients, optimizer states, activations, temporary/runtime buffers and other material training-memory components before declaring memory feasibility. Components that are not used by the selected training method must not be added merely by assumption.
Inputs: Training mode; parameter representation; gradient representation; optimizer; optimizer-state representation; activation configuration; runtime/framework buffers; distributed strategy
Condition: Training memory feasibility is evaluated from an incomplete set of applicable memory components
Output_Decision: INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE until all applicable training-memory components are identified
Source_Title: ZeRO: Memory Optimizations Toward Training Trillion Parameter Models
Exact_Page_Section_Table_Equation: §1 Extended Introduction; §3 Where Did All the Memory Go?; §3.1 Model States; §3.2 Residual Memory Consumption
Evidence: ZeRO separates training memory into model states—parameters, gradients and optimizer states—and residual states including activations, temporary buffers and fragmented memory.
Applicability: Full training and fine-tuning configurations where the listed states are material.
Limitations: Not every workload uses every component; exact memory depends on optimizer, precision, architecture and runtime.

Rule_Name: Parameter Memory Must Use the Selected Parameter Representation
Rule_Description: DSS must calculate or obtain parameter memory using the actual parameter representation/precision selected for training. It must not apply a fixed bytes-per-parameter assumption when the representation is unspecified.
Inputs: Parameter count; parameter dtype/precision; quantization/representation; training framework
Input_Source: Training workload specification + existing GPU formula
Condition: Parameter memory is estimated without an explicit parameter representation
Output_Decision: INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE until parameter representation is specified
Source_Title: Mixed Precision Training; ZeRO: Memory Optimizations Toward Training Trillion Parameter Models
Exact_Page_Section_Table_Equation: Mixed Precision Training: Abstract and mixed-precision training method; ZeRO §3.1 Model States
Evidence: Mixed Precision Training stores weights/activations/gradients in half precision while retaining a higher-precision weight copy for updates; ZeRO explicitly derives parameter-related memory from parameter count and representation.
Applicability: Training and fine-tuning with explicit numeric representation.
Limitations: Representation differs by framework and training method; no universal precision is assumed.

Rule_Name: Gradient Memory Must Be Accounted Separately From Parameter Memory
Rule_Description: DSS must treat gradients as a distinct training-memory component. The gradient representation may differ from the stored parameter representation and must be supplied by the selected training configuration.
Inputs: Parameter count; gradient dtype/precision; gradient accumulation strategy; distributed/sharding strategy
Condition: Gradient memory is omitted or automatically assumed equal to parameter memory without a defined representation
Output_Decision: INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE until gradient representation/strategy is established
Source_Title: ZeRO; Mixed Precision Training
Exact_Page_Section_Table_Equation: ZeRO §3.1 Model States; Mixed Precision Training: Abstract and method
Evidence: ZeRO treats gradients as a separate model-state category. Mixed Precision Training stores gradients in half precision in its proposed configuration, demonstrating that gradient representation is configuration dependent.
Applicability: Training configurations with explicit gradient representation.
Limitations: No universal gradient-to-parameter ratio is imposed.

Rule_Name: Optimizer-State Memory Must Follow the Selected Optimizer and Representation
Rule_Description: DSS must derive optimizer-state memory from the selected optimizer and its actual state representation. Optimizer-state memory must not be represented by one universal multiplier across optimizers or implementations.
Inputs: Optimizer type; optimizer state tensors; optimizer-state precision; master-weight representation; sharding strategy
Condition: Optimizer-state memory is assigned using a fixed multiplier independent of optimizer/configuration
Output_Decision: Use optimizer-specific state accounting; otherwise INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE
Source_Title: ZeRO; Mixed Precision Training
Exact_Page_Section_Table_Equation: ZeRO §3.1 Model States and §2.3 Training Optimizers; Mixed Precision Training method
Evidence: ZeRO explains that Adam maintains momentum and variance states and that optimizer-state memory can dominate parameter-related memory. Mixed Precision Training retains higher-precision copies needed for updates in its configuration.
Applicability: Any optimizer-based training configuration.
Limitations: Paper-specific optimizer-state sizes must remain configuration-specific; no universal multiplier is created.

Rule_Name: Activation Memory Must Be Evaluated Against Training Workload Characteristics
Rule_Description: DSS must treat activation memory as dependent on the actual training workload and architecture, including applicable batch size, sequence length, model depth/structure and activation representation. A fixed activation percentage of parameter memory must not be assumed.
Inputs: Batch size; sequence length; model architecture; number of layers; hidden dimensions; activation dtype; training strategy
Condition: Activation memory is represented using a universal fixed percentage or parameter-memory multiplier
Output_Decision: Use workload-specific activation evidence/model; otherwise INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE
Source_Title: ZeRO; Training Deep Nets with Sublinear Memory Cost
Exact_Page_Section_Table_Equation: ZeRO §3.2 Residual Memory Consumption; Training Deep Nets with Sublinear Memory Cost: Abstract, Introduction and memory-cost analysis
Evidence: ZeRO states that activation memory can be substantial and gives transformer-specific dependence on layers, hidden dimension, sequence length and batch size. Chen et al. focus on intermediate feature maps and gradients and show memory depends on network structure.
Applicability: Training workloads with material activation/intermediate-state memory.
Limitations: No universal activation formula or multiplier is imposed.

Rule_Name: Activation Checkpointing May Trade Memory Consumption for Recomputation
Rule_Description: If activation memory creates a capacity constraint and activation checkpointing/recomputation is applicable to the selected training framework, DSS may evaluate the checkpointed configuration as an alternative because the literature supports trading memory for additional computation.
Inputs: Activation memory pressure; checkpointing/recomputation availability; training framework; model architecture; recomputation configuration
Condition: Activation memory is a limiting component AND applicable checkpointing/recomputation is available
Output_Decision: Consider checkpointed configuration as a memory-reduction alternative; quantify its actual configuration-specific compute cost separately
Source_Title: Training Deep Nets with Sublinear Memory Cost; ZeRO
Exact_Page_Section_Table_Equation: Sublinear Memory: Abstract and memory optimization analysis; ZeRO §3.2 and §4.2.1
Evidence: Chen et al. explicitly trade recomputation for reduced intermediate-feature memory. ZeRO identifies activation checkpointing as a memory-reduction method and combines it with activation partitioning.
Applicability: Training workloads where the framework/model supports checkpointing or recomputation.
Limitations: No universal percentage reduction or compute overhead is assigned; the paper's numerical results are not generalized.

Rule_Name: Temporary Buffers and Memory Fragmentation Must Be Considered in Peak Training Memory
Rule_Description: DSS must not equate nominal free memory with guaranteed allocatable training memory when temporary buffers or memory fragmentation can affect allocation. Where the runtime exhibits these effects, peak training memory evidence must include them.
Inputs: Runtime/framework; temporary buffer requirements; allocator behavior; fragmentation evidence; measured peak memory
Condition: Training feasibility is declared solely from nominal capacity while temporary buffers or fragmentation are known to affect allocation
Output_Decision: Require peak/allocatable-memory evidence or return INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE
Source_Title: ZeRO: Memory Optimizations Toward Training Trillion Parameter Models
Exact_Page_Section_Table_Equation: §3.2 Residual Memory Consumption; discussion of temporary buffers and memory fragmentation
Evidence: ZeRO identifies temporary buffers and fragmented memory as residual-state contributors and notes allocation failure can occur even when total free memory appears sufficient because contiguous memory is unavailable.
Applicability: Large-model training and runtimes where temporary allocations/fragmentation are material.
Limitations: The catalogue does not contain measured runtime allocator/fragmentation fields; this is a workload/runtime evidence requirement.

Rule_Name: Mixed Precision Must Be Evaluated Per Memory Component
Rule_Description: When mixed precision is selected, DSS must identify the dtype/precision used for parameters, gradients, activations, master weights and optimizer states separately. Changing compute precision must not automatically be interpreted as changing every memory component identically.
Inputs: Parameter dtype; gradient dtype; activation dtype; master-weight dtype; optimizer-state dtype; framework mixed-precision configuration
Condition: A single precision label is used as though it determines every training-memory component
Output_Decision: Require component-level precision mapping before training-memory estimation
Source_Title: Mixed Precision Training; FP8-LM; PyTorch FSDP Documentation
Exact_Page_Section_Table_Equation: Mixed Precision Training: method; FP8-LM §2.2 FP8 Optimizer; PyTorch FSDP MixedPrecision API documentation
Evidence: Mixed Precision Training stores weights, activations and gradients in reduced precision while retaining a higher-precision weight copy. FSDP exposes separate parameter and gradient-reduction dtypes and keeps sharded parameters in full precision outside forward/backward in its documented configuration.
Applicability: Mixed-precision training and fine-tuning configurations.
Limitations: Exact component dtypes vary by framework and training strategy.

Rule_Name: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning Must Use Its Actual Trainable-State Configuration
Rule_Description: For parameter-efficient fine-tuning such as LoRA/QLoRA, DSS must distinguish frozen base-model storage from trainable adapter parameters and optimizer states instead of applying a full-parameter training memory model unchanged.
Inputs: Frozen base-model status; base-model representation; trainable adapter parameters; optimizer configuration; paged/offloaded optimizer setting
Condition: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning is selected but full-parameter training memory accounting is used unchanged
Output_Decision: Use configuration-specific fine-tuning memory accounting
Source_Title: QLoRA: Efficient Finetuning of Quantized LLMs
Exact_Page_Section_Table_Equation: Abstract; §3 QLoRA Finetuning; 4-bit NormalFloat Quantization; Paged Optimizers
Evidence: QLoRA freezes a 4-bit quantized pretrained model and trains low-rank adapters, while paged optimizers manage memory spikes. This is materially different from full-parameter full-precision training.
Applicability: QLoRA/LoRA-like parameter-efficient fine-tuning configurations.
Limitations: QLoRA's numerical model-size examples are study-specific and are not universal limits.

Rule_Name: Replicated Data-Parallel Training Must Be Evaluated Per Device
Rule_Description: When model states are replicated across data-parallel workers, DSS must compare the applicable replicated training-memory requirement against each participating device's available memory. Aggregate memory cannot be substituted for per-device capacity in this mode.
Inputs: Data-parallel strategy; per-device training-memory requirement; GPU_Memory_Per_Accelerator_GB; participating device count
Condition: Model states are replicated across devices AND per-device applicable training memory exceeds per-device available memory
Output_Decision: INFEASIBLE under the replicated data-parallel configuration
Source_Title: ZeRO; Part 0 Memory Catalogue Audit
Exact_Page_Section_Table_Equation: ZeRO §2.1 Data, Model and Pipeline Parallelism; §4.1 ZeRO-DP; §5 Deep Dive into ZeRO-DP
Evidence: ZeRO states that basic data parallelism replicates model states on every device and does not reduce memory per device.
Applicability: Replicated data-parallel training.
Limitations: Does not apply unchanged to sharded data parallelism such as ZeRO/FSDP.

Rule_Name: Sharded Training Requires an Explicit Per-Device State Distribution
Rule_Description: When ZeRO/FSDP or another sharding strategy is selected, DSS must use the documented state-distribution strategy to determine per-device memory; it must not assume that aggregate memory becomes linearly usable without verifying what is sharded and what is temporarily materialized.
Inputs: Sharding strategy; parameters sharded/replicated state; gradients sharded/replicated state; optimizer states sharded/replicated state; per-device GPU memory
Condition: Sharding is claimed but the distribution of parameters, gradients and optimizer states is not specified
Output_Decision: INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE until the sharding strategy and per-device state mapping are defined
Source_Title: ZeRO; PyTorch FullyShardedDataParallel Documentation
Exact_Page_Section_Table_Equation: ZeRO §4.1 and §5; PyTorch FSDP ShardingStrategy documentation
Evidence: ZeRO partitions optimizer states, gradients and parameters in cumulative stages. PyTorch documents FULL_SHARD, SHARD_GRAD_OP, NO_SHARD and HYBRID_SHARD with different state distribution.
Applicability: ZeRO/FSDP and equivalent distributed training strategies.
Limitations: Exact peak memory depends on wrapping, gather/reshard behavior and runtime configuration.

Rule_Name: Sharded Training Must Account for Temporary Unsharded Parameters During Computation
Rule_Description: For sharded training implementations that all-gather parameters for forward/backward computation, DSS must evaluate peak per-device memory using the configuration's temporary unsharded materialization rather than only the persistent shard size.
Inputs: Sharding strategy; FSDP/ZeRO wrapping granularity; parameter shard size; gathered parameter size; activation memory; per-device GPU memory
Condition: Peak memory is estimated only from persistent shards while the implementation temporarily materializes unsharded parameters
Output_Decision: Use peak-memory behavior of the selected sharding implementation or return INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE
Source_Title: PyTorch FullyShardedDataParallel Documentation; ZeRO
Exact_Page_Section_Table_Equation: PyTorch FSDP ShardingStrategy FULL_SHARD documentation; ZeRO §5 Deep Dive into ZeRO-DP
Evidence: PyTorch documents that FULL_SHARD unshards parameters before forward/backward and reshards afterward; this means transient full parameters can contribute to peak device memory.
Applicability: FSDP FULL_SHARD and equivalent gather/reshard implementations.
Limitations: Peak behavior depends on wrapping granularity and runtime controls; no universal peak multiplier is assumed.

Rule_Name: CPU-Offloaded Training Must Verify Host-Memory Capacity and Placement
Rule_Description: When training states are offloaded from accelerator memory to CPU memory, DSS must verify that the selected host-memory pool can accommodate the offloaded states and that the workload explicitly uses CPU offload. GPU capacity alone is not sufficient evidence of feasibility.
Inputs: CPU-offload configuration; offloaded parameter/gradient/optimizer states; System_Memory_GB; System_Memory_Status; GPU memory; offload runtime
Condition: CPU offload is enabled AND host-memory capacity/placement for offloaded states is not established
Output_Decision: INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE until host-memory capacity and offload placement are verified
Source_Title: Part 0 Memory Catalogue Audit; ZeRO-Offload; ZeRO-Infinity; PyTorch FSDP Documentation
Exact_Page_Section_Table_Equation: ZeRO-Offload Abstract; ZeRO-Infinity Abstract/heterogeneous memory hierarchy; PyTorch FSDP CPUOffload documentation; Part 0 System_Memory_GB field
Evidence: ZeRO-Offload moves training data/compute to CPU to save GPU memory. ZeRO-Infinity uses GPU, CPU and NVMe memory as a hierarchy. PyTorch FSDP documents CPU parameter/gradient offload. Therefore offloaded training shifts memory demand to another pool rather than eliminating it.
Applicability: Training configurations with CPU offload or heterogeneous memory placement.
Limitations: Offload performance/data movement is outside this Part 2 memory-capacity rule; no host-memory safety margin is imposed.

Rule_Name: Training Memory Feasibility Must Use the Selected Placement Granularity
Rule_Description: After training-memory components are characterized, DSS must compare the applicable per-device requirement with per-device available memory for replicated/sharded device execution, and use host memory only for explicitly offloaded states. Aggregate capacity may be reported separately but cannot replace the applicable per-device check.
Inputs: Required training memory by component and placement; GPU_Memory_Per_Accelerator_GB; System_Memory_GB; distribution strategy; offload strategy
Input_Source: Part 1 feasibility foundation + research literature + hardware catalogue
Condition: Training feasibility is evaluated using aggregate capacity while the selected strategy imposes per-device or separate host-memory constraints
Output_Decision: INFEASIBLE or INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE until the required placement granularity is satisfied
Source_Title: Part 0 Memory Catalogue Audit; ZeRO; PyTorch FSDP Documentation
Exact_Page_Section_Table_Equation: Part 1 MEM-P1-F01; ZeRO §4–§5; PyTorch FSDP ShardingStrategy
Evidence: ZeRO distinguishes per-device replicated/sharded state memory; FSDP documents different per-rank state distributions. Part 1 already establishes that applicable memory must be compared at the correct placement granularity.
Applicability: All training and fine-tuning configurations evaluated by DSS.
Limitations: The rule does not estimate the component requirements; it consumes component-specific requirements supplied by the workload/training-memory layer.

Rule_Name: Inference Model Memory Must Use the Actual Stored Weight Representation
Rule_Description: DSS must determine inference model/weight memory from the target parameter representation actually used for serving. Parameter count alone is insufficient when stored precision, quantization, packing, or representation is unspecified.
Inputs: Parameter count; stored weight precision; quantization/representation; model format
Input_Source: Inference workload specification + existing GPU/Workload formula book
Condition: Stored weight representation is missing or unspecified
Output_Decision: INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE until stored representation is specified
Source_Title: SmoothQuant; FlexGen
Organisation: Xiao et al.; Sheng et al.
Exact_Page_Section_Table_Equation: SmoothQuant: Abstract; §3–§4; FlexGen: §4 Offloading Strategy
Evidence: Inference memory depends on how weights are represented and placed; FlexGen explicitly models tensor placement across GPU/CPU/disk and SmoothQuant studies W8A8 inference quantization.
Applicability: LLM and transformer inference/serving where model representation is explicitly known.
Limitations: Exact memory also depends on framework packing, metadata, alignment and other runtime allocations.

Rule_Name: Stored Weight Precision Must Be Distinguished From Compute and Activation Precision
Rule_Description: DSS must represent stored weight precision separately from compute precision and activation precision. A lower-precision weight representation must not automatically be treated as changing every other inference-memory component.
Inputs: Stored weight precision; compute precision; activation precision; runtime configuration
Condition: Weight precision is changed but compute/activation precision is assumed to change automatically
Output_Decision: REQUIRE EXPLICIT COMPONENT PRECISIONS
Source_Title: SmoothQuant; NVIDIA TensorRT Quantization Schemes
Exact_Page_Section_Table_Equation: SmoothQuant: Abstract; §3; NVIDIA TensorRT: Quantization Schemes, Table 14
Evidence: SmoothQuant explicitly studies W8A8 weights and activations; TensorRT documents separate quantization representations and scale types for weights and activations.
Applicability: Inference deployments using mixed or quantized representations.
Limitations: Exact component dtypes are framework/model dependent; vendor support is capability evidence, not a universal configuration.

Rule_Name: Quantized Inference Memory Must Preserve the Actual Quantization Configuration
Rule_Description: DSS may use quantization to represent model weights or other inference tensors more compactly, but the selected scheme, bit width, packing/scales and runtime support must be recorded rather than applying a universal memory-reduction percentage.
Inputs: Quantization method; weight bit width; activation bit width; packing; scale representation; runtime/backend
Condition: Quantized representation is used without an explicit scheme or runtime support
Output_Decision: INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE until quantization configuration is explicit
Source_Title: SmoothQuant; NVIDIA TensorRT Quantization Schemes; FlexGen
Organisation: Xiao et al.; NVIDIA; Sheng et al.
Exact_Page_Section_Table_Equation: SmoothQuant: Abstract; §3–§4; TensorRT: Quantization Schemes/Table 14; FlexGen: §4
Evidence: Quantization is configuration-specific; FlexGen also uses compressed weights/cache in a particular latency-insensitive serving setup.
Applicability: Specific model/backend/hardware configurations where quantization support is verified.
Limitations: Paper-specific memory/accuracy results must not become DSS-wide thresholds.

Rule_Name: Inference Memory Must Include Dynamic KV Cache Where the Serving Model Uses Attention KV State
Rule_Description: For autoregressive transformer serving that retains attention key/value state, DSS must treat KV cache as a dynamic memory component in addition to model weights.
Inputs: Model architecture; KV-cache usage; context length; batch/concurrency; KV precision
Input_Source: Inference workload specification + existing GPU/Workload formula book
Condition: Serving configuration uses a KV cache but feasibility evaluates only model weights
Output_Decision: INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE until KV-cache demand is represented
Source_Title: PagedAttention; KIVI
Organisation: Kwon et al.; Liu et al.
Exact_Page_Section_Table_Equation: PagedAttention: p.1 Fig.1; §3; §4.1; KIVI: Abstract; §2–§3
Evidence: PagedAttention identifies KV cache as a large, dynamically allocated serving state; KIVI identifies KV cache as a major memory demand that grows with batch size and context length.
Applicability: Autoregressive transformer/LLM serving with cached attention states.
Limitations: Not every inference architecture uses the same KV-cache structure; exact cache layout is architecture/framework dependent.

Rule_Name: KV Cache Demand Must Preserve Context, Batch, and Concurrency Dependencies
Rule_Description: DSS must evaluate KV-cache demand using the actual context/sequence and concurrent-request configuration. It must not substitute a fixed KV-cache multiplier or fixed percentage of model memory.
Inputs: Layers; KV heads; head dimension; context/tokens; batch or concurrent requests; KV element precision
Input_Source: Inference workload specification + existing KV-cache formula
Condition: Context/concurrency is unspecified for a serving configuration whose KV cache is dynamic
Output_Decision: INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE for a quantitative KV-cache feasibility result
Source_Title: PagedAttention; KIVI
Organisation: Kwon et al.; Liu et al.
Exact_Page_Section_Table_Equation: PagedAttention: p.1 Fig.1; §3; §4.1; KIVI: Abstract
Evidence: Both papers connect serving memory pressure to dynamic KV-cache state; KIVI explicitly reports increased memory demand with larger batch sizes and longer contexts.
Applicability: LLM/transformer serving where KV-cache dimensions follow the selected model architecture.
Limitations: Exact scaling depends on architecture, attention type, cache precision and serving implementation.

Rule_Name: KV Cache Precision Must Be Modeled Separately From Weight Precision
Rule_Description: DSS must record KV-cache precision independently when the serving framework allows a different cache representation from model weights. Weight quantization alone must not be treated as evidence that KV-cache memory changed.
Inputs: Weight precision; KV-cache precision; quantization method; runtime/backend
Condition: KV-cache precision is absent while a quantitative KV-cache estimate is required
Output_Decision: INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE until KV-cache representation is specified
Source_Title: KIVI; NVIDIA TensorRT Quantization Schemes
Exact_Page_Section_Table_Equation: KIVI: Abstract; §3; TensorRT: Quantization Schemes
Evidence: KIVI is specifically a KV-cache quantization method, demonstrating that cache precision is an independent inference-memory design dimension.
Applicability: Serving systems that implement quantized KV-cache storage.
Limitations: KIVI results are model/configuration-specific; no universal quality or memory reduction should be assumed.

Rule_Name: Demand-Paged or Block-Based KV Allocation Must Be Distinguished From Raw KV-Byte Demand
Rule_Description: DSS should distinguish the logical KV-cache requirement from the serving system's allocation/fragmentation behavior. A memory-management technique such as PagedAttention can change utilization and fragmentation without changing the underlying logical token state required by the model.
Inputs: Logical KV-cache demand; allocation strategy; block/page size; request lengths; memory-management policy
Condition: KV-cache feasibility assumes all allocated KV memory is a single perfectly packed logical tensor
Output_Decision: REQUIRE ALLOCATION STRATEGY / RETURN INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE FOR PEAK CAPACITY CLAIM
Source_Title: PagedAttention; vLLM Parallelism and Scaling
Exact_Page_Section_Table_Equation: PagedAttention: p.1 Fig.1; §4.1; vLLM docs: Parallelism and Scaling, KV cache size/concurrency discussion
Evidence: PagedAttention uses block-level on-demand allocation to reduce fragmentation; vLLM reports GPU KV-cache capacity and concurrency as serving configuration outputs.
Applicability: Serving frameworks with explicit KV-cache memory managers.
Limitations: Implementation-specific fragmentation, block sizing and scheduler behavior must be measured/configured.

Rule_Name: Online Inference Memory Must Account for Dynamic Request Concurrency
Rule_Description: For latency-sensitive or interactive serving, DSS must evaluate memory against the configured or measured concurrent-request workload rather than using a single-request memory estimate.
Inputs: Serving mode; concurrency; request arrival/queue behavior; context length; KV-cache demand
Condition: Online serving is evaluated with a single-request memory footprint while concurrency is materially above one
Output_Decision: INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE for online peak-memory feasibility
Source_Title: PagedAttention; KIVI; vLLM
Organisation: Kwon et al.; Liu et al.; vLLM project
Exact_Page_Section_Table_Equation: PagedAttention: p.1 Fig.1; §3; KIVI: Abstract; vLLM docs: GPU KV cache size and maximum concurrency
Evidence: Serving memory is dynamic across requests; vLLM exposes KV-cache capacity and concurrency as runtime planning quantities.
Applicability: Online/interactive serving with dynamic batching or concurrent requests.
Limitations: Concurrency distributions are workload-specific; a peak concurrency value should come from the workload/SLA rather than a universal threshold.

Rule_Name: Batch Inference Memory Must Preserve Batch and Sequence Configuration
Rule_Description: For latency-insensitive or offline/batch inference, DSS must model the selected batch size and sequence/input-output configuration rather than applying the online-serving concurrency rule unchanged.
Inputs: Serving mode; batch size; input length; output length; model representation; KV-cache usage
Condition: Batch/offline inference is evaluated without the selected batch/sequence configuration
Output_Decision: INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE for quantitative batch-memory feasibility
Source_Title: FlexGen; PagedAttention
Organisation: Sheng et al.; Kwon et al.
Exact_Page_Section_Table_Equation: FlexGen: Introduction; §3 Memory Analysis; §4; PagedAttention: §3
Evidence: FlexGen explicitly targets latency-insensitive batched generation and analyzes memory under batch/input/output configurations; PagedAttention links batching to KV-cache management.
Applicability: Offline or throughput-oriented batch inference.
Limitations: The relationship between batch size and peak memory depends on architecture, cache policy, offloading and runtime.

Rule_Name: Inference Feasibility Must Include Runtime, Workspace, and Temporary Memory Beyond Weights and KV Cache
Rule_Description: DSS must not declare inference memory feasible from model weights and KV cache alone when the selected runtime/framework requires additional activations, workspace, execution buffers, scheduler buffers or other allocations.
Inputs: Model weights; KV cache; runtime/framework; workspace; temporary buffers; serving framework configuration
Input_Source: Inference runtime configuration + existing total-inference formula
Condition: Runtime memory is omitted from a configuration where the runtime exposes or requires additional allocations
Output_Decision: INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE until applicable runtime memory is represented or measured
Source_Title: PagedAttention; FlexGen; NVIDIA TensorRT
Organisation: Kwon et al.; Sheng et al.; NVIDIA
Exact_Page_Section_Table_Equation: PagedAttention: p.1 Fig.1 (Others); FlexGen: §4; TensorRT: quantization/runtime documentation
Evidence: PagedAttention's memory layout includes other ephemeral allocations beyond parameters and KV cache; FlexGen models additional tensor movement/storage; TensorRT documents runtime-supported execution representations.
Applicability: Inference deployments using GPU runtime/frameworks or serving engines.
Limitations: Exact runtime overhead is framework/model dependent; no fixed percentage is assigned.

Rule_Name: Single-GPU Inference Must Fit All Applicable Inference Memory Components
Rule_Description: For single-GPU inference, DSS must compare total applicable inference memory—not only model weights—against the applicable per-accelerator memory capacity.
Inputs: Model weight memory; KV cache; runtime memory; applicable GPU memory capacity
Condition: Total applicable inference memory exceeds the candidate GPU's applicable memory capacity
Output_Decision: INFEASIBLE — inference configuration does not fit selected GPU memory capacity
Source_Title: vLLM; NVIDIA H100; AMD Instinct MI300X
Version_Year: current documentation; current product docs; current product docs
Exact_Page_Section_Table_Equation: vLLM docs: Parallelism and Scaling; NVIDIA H100 Product Specifications; AMD MI300X GPU Specifications
Evidence: Vendor documents establish hardware memory capacity; vLLM documents selecting more GPUs/nodes when sufficient GPU memory is needed.
Applicability: Candidate hardware records with verified applicable GPU memory capacity.
Limitations: Available capacity must reflect the exact hardware/entity level and runtime allocation; capacity is not equivalent to usable workload memory without runtime evidence.

Rule_Name: Multi-GPU Inference Must Be Evaluated Per Device and Placement Strategy
Rule_Description: DSS must evaluate the amount of model/runtime/KV state assigned to each GPU under the selected inference strategy. Aggregate GPU memory must not be treated as one shared pool.
Inputs: GPU count; per-GPU memory; aggregate memory; tensor/pipeline/model parallel strategy; per-device placement
Input_Source: GPU/server catalogue + serving configuration + technical documentation
Condition: Aggregate GPU memory is sufficient but one or more devices cannot hold their assigned inference state
Output_Decision: INFEASIBLE — per-device placement requirement is not satisfied
Source_Title: vLLM Parallelism and Scaling; DeepSpeed Inference; NVIDIA H100; AMD MI300X
Version_Year: current documentation; current documentation; current product docs; current product docs
Exact_Page_Section_Table_Equation: vLLM: Parallelism and Scaling; DeepSpeed: Inference Overview; vendor GPU specifications
Evidence: vLLM and DeepSpeed describe model-parallel inference to fit models across GPUs; vendor sources provide per-device and platform memory capabilities.
Applicability: Tensor/pipeline/model-parallel or other explicitly partitioned multi-GPU inference.
Limitations: Exact per-device distribution depends on model architecture, parallelism degree, framework and implementation.

Rule_Name: Tensor, Pipeline, or Model Parallel Inference Must Use an Explicit Placement Configuration
Rule_Description: DSS must record the selected model/tensor/pipeline parallel degree and use that placement when evaluating per-device inference memory. GPU count alone does not determine state placement.
Inputs: Parallelism strategy; tensor-parallel degree; pipeline-parallel degree; model architecture; GPU topology
Condition: Multi-GPU inference is specified only by GPU count without a placement strategy
Output_Decision: INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE for per-device inference-memory feasibility
Source_Title: vLLM Parallelism and Scaling; DeepSpeed Inference
Exact_Page_Section_Table_Equation: vLLM: Parallelism and Scaling; DeepSpeed: Inference Overview
Evidence: vLLM distinguishes single-GPU, tensor-parallel and tensor+pipeline-parallel serving; DeepSpeed exposes model-parallel degree and partitions the model accordingly.
Applicability: Multi-GPU model serving.
Limitations: Framework support and optimal placement depend on model architecture and hardware topology; no universal parallelism degree is assigned.

Rule_Name: Replicated Inference and Sharded Inference Must Be Represented Differently
Rule_Description: DSS must distinguish replicated model replicas from sharded/model-parallel placement because the memory required per GPU differs. Replicating a model does not create a shared aggregate memory pool.
Inputs: Replication/sharding mode; replica count; parallelism degree; per-device state assignment; GPU memory
Condition: Inference architecture is labeled multi-GPU without distinguishing replication from sharding
Output_Decision: INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE for per-device memory evaluation
Source_Title: vLLM Parallelism and Scaling; DeepSpeed Inference
Exact_Page_Section_Table_Equation: vLLM: single-model replica distributed inference strategies; DeepSpeed: model parallelism and partitioning
Evidence: The two frameworks explicitly distinguish single-model distributed inference/model parallelism from multiple model replicas or placement configurations.
Applicability: Distributed inference architectures where replica and model-parallel modes can differ.
Limitations: Exact memory duplication/sharding behavior is framework-specific and must be taken from the selected serving configuration.

Rule_Name: CPU-Offloaded Inference Must Verify Host-Memory Capacity and Placement
Rule_Description: If inference uses CPU or other host-side offload, DSS must move the relevant state to the corresponding memory pool and verify host capacity; offload changes placement rather than removing the memory requirement.
Inputs: Offloaded tensor/state; host-memory capacity; GPU memory; offload strategy; runtime
Input_Source: Serving framework configuration + server/memory catalogue + research literature
Condition: GPU memory is treated as sufficient only because state is offloaded, without checking host-side capacity
Output_Decision: INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE until offloaded-state placement and host capacity are verified
Source_Title: FlexGen; DeepSpeed Inference
Exact_Page_Section_Table_Equation: FlexGen: §4 Offloading Strategy; DeepSpeed: Inference Overview
Evidence: FlexGen explicitly models GPU/CPU/disk memory as a hierarchy and searches tensor placement; DeepSpeed supports model parallelism and inference configuration across multiple GPUs.
Applicability: Inference deployments using CPU/host offload or heterogeneous memory placement.
Limitations: Host-memory bandwidth, transfer overhead and exact offloaded tensors are workload/framework dependent.

Rule_Name: Quantization May Be Used as a Memory-Fit Strategy Only With Explicit Configuration and Hardware Support
Rule_Description: DSS may consider quantization as a candidate strategy when an unquantized model does not fit, but the decision must preserve the selected quantization scheme, supported hardware/runtime, and model-specific evidence.
Inputs: Unquantized memory; quantized representation; hardware support; runtime/backend; model accuracy constraints
Input_Source: Inference candidate configuration + vendor/technical documentation + research
Condition: Quantization is proposed solely from an assumed universal percentage reduction
Output_Decision: INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE for quantitative fit claim
Source_Title: SmoothQuant; KIVI; NVIDIA TensorRT Quantization Schemes
Organisation: Xiao et al.; Liu et al.; NVIDIA
Exact_Page_Section_Table_Equation: SmoothQuant: Abstract; KIVI: Abstract; TensorRT: Quantization Schemes/Table 14
Evidence: Research demonstrates memory reductions for specific quantization configurations, while TensorRT documents supported quantization representations; these do not define a universal reduction factor.
Applicability: Specific models, quantization schemes, and hardware/runtime combinations.
Limitations: Accuracy, kernel support, scale metadata and packing can alter practical memory and performance; no universal percentage is used.

Rule_Name: Inference Memory Bottleneck Must Be Attributed to a Verified Memory Pressure Condition
Rule_Description: DSS should classify an inference-memory bottleneck only when evidence shows that model weights, KV cache, runtime memory, concurrency/context, or per-device placement is the limiting capacity condition.
Inputs: Required memory components; measured/estimated peak memory; applicable capacity; workload configuration; placement
Input_Source: Runtime measurement or validated workload model + catalogue capacity
Condition: A bottleneck label is assigned without identifying the memory component or capacity failure
Output_Decision: INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE — do not classify bottleneck without component/capacity evidence
Source_Title: PagedAttention; FlexGen
Organisation: Kwon et al.; Sheng et al.
Exact_Page_Section_Table_Equation: PagedAttention: §3; FlexGen: §3 Memory Analysis; §4
Evidence: Both works identify concrete memory-pressure mechanisms rather than a universal bottleneck threshold; DSS should retain the specific component and workload context.
Applicability: Any inference workload where memory pressure can be profiled or modeled.
Limitations: Missing evidence is not equivalent to infeasibility.

Rule_Name: Inference Memory Feasibility Must Compare Total Applicable Requirement With Applicable Available Capacity
Rule_Description: DSS must evaluate the full applicable inference-memory requirement against the applicable memory capacity at the placement granularity required by the serving strategy. If required workload-specific memory is unavailable, the system must return INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE rather than assume feasibility.
Inputs: Model weight memory; KV cache; runtime memory; placement; per-device capacity; host capacity if offloaded
Input_Source: Existing GPU/Workload formulas + Part 1 capacity gate + catalogue fields
Condition: Any required component is unknown, or required applicable memory exceeds applicable capacity
Output_Decision: INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE if required demand is unknown; otherwise INFEASIBLE when verified demand exceeds applicable capacity
Source_Title: vLLM Parallelism and Scaling; PagedAttention
Exact_Page_Section_Table_Equation: vLLM: Parallelism and Scaling; PagedAttention: p.1 Fig.1; §3
Evidence: The feasibility decision must consider model memory plus dynamic serving memory and placement; vLLM explicitly plans GPU count/node count around sufficient GPU memory.
Applicability: All inference modes; placement granularity must follow the selected architecture.
Limitations: Available catalogue capacity is a hardware capability, not necessarily usable runtime memory; workload/runtime evidence may be required.

Rule_Name: Theoretical Bandwidth Must Not Be Treated as Guaranteed Workload Bandwidth
Rule_Description: Treat catalogue/vendor peak or theoretical memory bandwidth as a hardware capability value, not as guaranteed application bandwidth. Use measured or validated sustained bandwidth when making workload feasibility decisions.
Inputs: Memory_Bandwidth_GBps; Memory_Bandwidth_Status; workload measurement
Input_Source: Memory catalogue; GPU/CPU catalogue; vendor documentation
Condition: Only theoretical/specification bandwidth is available and no comparable workload/benchmark measurement exists
Output_Decision: CLASSIFY AS THEORETICAL-ONLY EVIDENCE
Source_Title: Sustainable Memory Bandwidth in Current High Performance Computers
Exact_Page_Section_Table_Equation: Discussion of sustainable memory bandwidth and application performance
Evidence: The paper distinguishes sustainable memory bandwidth obtainable by user codes from hardware-level specifications and emphasizes that architectural factors affect sustainable bandwidth.
Applicability: General memory-bandwidth planning; especially low-compute-density/vector-style workloads.
Limitations: Historical study; measured behavior is platform/workload dependent and must not be generalized numerically.

Rule_Name: Measured Bandwidth Should Be Derived From Data Transferred Over Measurement Time
Rule_Description: When transferred data and measurement duration are available and consistently scoped, measured bandwidth can be calculated from the observed data movement and elapsed measurement time.
Inputs: D_transferred; T_measurement
Condition: Transferred data and measurement interval are both defined with matching scope and units
Output_Decision: USE CPU-P3-F01 FOR MEASURED BANDWIDTH
Source_Title: Optimizing Memory Bandwidth on Stream Triad
Exact_Page_Section_Table_Equation: Introduction; STREAM benchmark measurement methodology
Evidence: Intel describes STREAM as a benchmark for measuring sustainable memory bandwidth and specifies its measured transfer-rate methodology.
Applicability: Measured CPU/host bandwidth and comparable memory-bandwidth benchmark measurements.
Limitations: Transfer accounting must match benchmark/application methodology; cache traffic and measurement scope affect interpretation.

Rule_Name: Workload Bandwidth Demand May Be Derived From Data Movement Per Unit and Processing Rate
Rule_Description: Represent workload-specific memory-bandwidth demand from a defined amount of memory traffic per processed unit multiplied by the processing rate, only when the bytes-per-unit quantity is measured or otherwise explicitly established.
Inputs: B_per_unit; R_units
Condition: Bytes transferred per workload unit and units processed per second are both defined consistently
Output_Decision: USE CPU-P3-F03 FOR WORKLOAD BANDWIDTH DEMAND
Source_Title: Memory Bandwidth Prediction in NUMA Architecture Using Supervised Machine Learning
Exact_Page_Section_Table_Equation: Abstract; bandwidth expressed as total transferred data / execution time
Evidence: The paper expresses memory bandwidth as total transferred data divided by execution time and shows that bandwidth varies with problem size and processor/thread count.
Applicability: Workloads where data movement per unit can be measured or defined and processing rate is known.
Limitations: Do not invent bytes-per-sample, bytes-per-token, or similar constants; cache, NUMA and hidden traffic can change actual movement.

Rule_Name: Benchmark Bandwidth Must Retain Hardware, Workload, Benchmark, and Configuration Context
Rule_Description: Store benchmark bandwidth together with the platform, benchmark/kernel, configuration, and measurement context before using it as evidence for DSS planning.
Inputs: Benchmark bandwidth; benchmark name; hardware; configuration; workload context
Condition: Benchmark result is available but context metadata is incomplete
Output_Decision: CLASSIFY AS CONTEXT-LIMITED EVIDENCE UNTIL CONTEXT IS COMPLETE
Source_Title: STREAM Benchmark Reference Information
Organisation: John D. McCalpin / University of Virginia
Exact_Page_Section_Table_Equation: STREAM Benchmark Reference Information; standard vs tuned results
Evidence: STREAM maintains separate standard and tuned result categories and requires benchmark citation/context for specific results.
Applicability: Any benchmark result used to estimate or validate memory bandwidth.
Limitations: STREAM is synthetic and does not represent every application access pattern.

Rule_Name: Memory Access Pattern Must Be Considered When Interpreting Achieved Bandwidth
Rule_Description: Interpret achieved bandwidth in the context of sequential/streaming, reuse, cache behavior, and other access-pattern characteristics rather than treating one measured bandwidth as access-pattern independent.
Inputs: Access pattern; memory traffic; cache/reuse behavior; achieved bandwidth
Condition: Access-pattern or reuse characteristics differ materially from the benchmark used as the bandwidth reference
Output_Decision: REQUIRE COMPARABLE ACCESS-PATTERN EVIDENCE
Source_Title: Roofline: An Insightful Visual Performance Model for Multicore Architectures
Exact_Page_Section_Table_Equation: Performance Models / Roofline discussion of operational intensity, memory traffic, and memory affinity
Evidence: Roofline relates performance to operational intensity and memory traffic, and discusses memory-affinity and access-pattern effects on performance.
Applicability: CPU/GPU kernels where memory traffic and reuse materially affect performance.
Limitations: Roofline is a performance model; it does not by itself predict exact sustained bandwidth for arbitrary applications.

Rule_Name: Memory Locality Should Be Preserved Where the Platform Uses NUMA Memory Domains
Rule_Description: For NUMA systems, place frequently accessed memory as close as practical to the executing CPU/thread or applicable device and preserve the topology used by the validated configuration.
Inputs: Memory_Channels; Memory_Configuration; CPU/socket topology; thread/process placement
Condition: Workload execution crosses NUMA domains and evidence indicates locality-sensitive memory traffic
Output_Decision: FLAG LOCALITY AS A MEMORY-PERFORMANCE CONSTRAINT
Source_Title: NUMA-Caffe: NUMA-Aware Deep Learning Neural Networks
Exact_Page_Section_Table_Equation: Introduction and NUMA-aware design discussion; remote NUMA-domain memory accesses
Evidence: NUMA-Caffe reports that CPU-based DNN frameworks can suffer from remote NUMA-domain memory accesses and proposes NUMA-aware design to improve scalability.
Applicability: CPU-based DNN workloads on multi-socket/multi-NUMA systems.
Limitations: No universal remote-memory slowdown is asserted; effect depends on topology, access pattern, framework and workload.

Rule_Name: Remote NUMA Access Must Not Be Assigned a Universal Performance Penalty
Rule_Description: Classify remote-memory access as a topology/locality concern when supported by platform topology or measurements, but do not convert one platform's measured slowdown into a universal percentage.
Inputs: NUMA topology; measured local/remote bandwidth or latency; CPU affinity
Condition: Remote/non-local memory access is observed or required
Output_Decision: REQUIRE PLATFORM-SPECIFIC LOCALITY EVIDENCE
Source_Title: NUMA-Caffe: NUMA-Aware Deep Learning Neural Networks
Exact_Page_Section_Table_Equation: Introduction and NUMA-aware design discussion; remote NUMA-domain memory accesses
Evidence: The study identifies remote NUMA-domain accesses as a source of long memory latency and poor scalability in CPU DNN execution.
Applicability: Multi-socket CPU/DNN workloads with NUMA domains.
Limitations: Measured effects are platform- and workload-specific; no universal percentage is used.

Rule_Name: Memory Bandwidth Should Be Evaluated Against Workload Size and Thread/Processor Configuration
Rule_Description: Do not assume a single bandwidth value across all problem sizes or thread counts. Use measurements or validated models for the target problem-size and parallel configuration.
Inputs: Problem size; thread count; processor count; measured bandwidth
Condition: Target workload problem size or parallel configuration differs from the configuration used to obtain the bandwidth reference
Output_Decision: REQUIRE CONFIGURATION-MATCHED BANDWIDTH EVIDENCE
Source_Title: Memory Bandwidth Prediction in NUMA Architecture Using Supervised Machine Learning
Exact_Page_Section_Table_Equation: Abstract; bandwidth changes with problem size and number of processors/threads
Evidence: The study states that memory bandwidth changes with problem size and number of processors/threads and predicts bandwidth using those dimensions.
Applicability: NUMA/HPC workloads where problem size and parallelism affect traffic.
Limitations: Prediction quality depends on training data coverage; not a universal bandwidth equation.

Rule_Name: CPU Memory Bandwidth Capability Must Be Interpreted With the Actual Memory Configuration
Rule_Description: Use CPU/server memory-channel and configuration fields to identify the applicable host-memory bandwidth capability, while recognizing that achieved bandwidth depends on configuration and software.
Inputs: Memory_Channels; Memory_Type; Memory_Configuration; Memory_Bandwidth_GBps
Condition: CPU/platform memory configuration is known
Output_Decision: USE APPLICABLE CPU/PLATFORM BANDWIDTH CAPABILITY AS HARDWARE INPUT
Source_Title: Measuring Memory Bandwidth — Intel Xeon Processor 7500 Platform
Exact_Page_Section_Table_Equation: Configuration guidance for STREAM on Xeon 7500/6500 platform; DIMM rank/channel population
Evidence: Intel documents that memory-channel population and DIMM configuration affect STREAM results and that platform/software configuration must be set appropriately.
Applicability: CPU/server platforms where channel and DIMM configuration is represented.
Limitations: The cited platform is historical; configuration effects must be checked against the actual server/CPU generation.

Rule_Name: Memory Channel Population and DIMM Configuration Must Be Preserved as Platform-Specific Inputs
Rule_Description: When bandwidth evidence depends on populated channels, DIMMs per channel, memory speed, or socket configuration, retain those configuration details when applying the result.
Inputs: Memory_Channels; Memory_Configuration; Memory_Speed_MTps
Condition: Bandwidth evidence was produced under a specified channel/DIMM configuration
Output_Decision: ONLY APPLY RESULT TO COMPATIBLE MEMORY CONFIGURATION
Source_Title: Measuring Memory Bandwidth — Intel Xeon Processor 7500 Platform
Exact_Page_Section_Table_Equation: Configuration guidance for STREAM on Xeon 7500/6500 platform; DIMM rank/channel population
Evidence: Intel reports measurable STREAM differences for DIMM rank/channel population and states that populating all channels is required for best results on the studied platform.
Applicability: The cited Intel Xeon 7500/6500 platform and similar cases only after configuration compatibility is verified.
Limitations: Do not generalize the numerical improvement to all servers.

Rule_Name: GPU Peak Memory Bandwidth Is a Hardware Capability Input, Not a Guaranteed Application Rate
Rule_Description: Use GPU Memory_Bandwidth_GBps as a theoretical/peak hardware capability unless a comparable achieved workload measurement is available.
Inputs: Memory_Bandwidth_GBps; Memory_Bandwidth_Status
Condition: Only peak/theoretical GPU bandwidth is available
Output_Decision: CLASSIFY BANDWIDTH AS THEORETICAL-ONLY FOR WORKLOAD FEASIBILITY
Source_Title: NVIDIA H100 Tensor Core GPU / NVIDIA-Certified Computing Platforms
Exact_Page_Section_Table_Equation: NVIDIA H100 platform specifications; 3.35 TB/s memory bandwidth per GPU
Evidence: NVIDIA publishes 3.35 TB/s memory bandwidth per H100 GPU as a hardware specification in the referenced platform context.
Applicability: NVIDIA H100-class hardware capability representation.
Limitations: Peak specification is not an application guarantee; workload, access pattern and achieved traffic must be validated separately.

Rule_Name: GPU Memory-Bandwidth Analysis Must Preserve the Accelerator and Measurement Scope
Rule_Description: For GPU bandwidth evidence, preserve accelerator model, memory technology, operation/kernel, data type where relevant, and whether the value is peak specification or achieved measurement.
Inputs: GPU model; Memory_Type; Memory_Bandwidth_GBps; workload/kernel; measurement scope
Condition: Bandwidth result or specification is being mapped to a target GPU
Output_Decision: REQUIRE MATCHED GPU AND MEASUREMENT SCOPE
Source_Title: AMD Instinct MI300X Accelerators
Exact_Page_Section_Table_Equation: AMD Instinct MI300X Accelerators; GPU Memory section
Evidence: AMD lists 192 GB HBM3 and 5.3 TB/s peak memory bandwidth for MI300X, demonstrating that memory type and accelerator identity are part of the hardware context.
Applicability: AMD MI300X hardware capability representation.
Limitations: Peak theoretical bandwidth is not sustained workload bandwidth.

Rule_Name: A Memory-Bandwidth Bottleneck Should Be Supported by Measured or Profiling Evidence
Rule_Description: Classify a workload as memory-bandwidth constrained only when measurements, profiling counters, roofline analysis, or comparable benchmark evidence indicate that memory traffic/bandwidth is limiting performance.
Inputs: Achieved bandwidth; memory traffic; operational intensity; profiling counters; performance
Condition: Evidence identifies memory bandwidth as a limiting performance ceiling
Output_Decision: CLASSIFY AS MEMORY-BANDWIDTH BOTTLENECK
Source_Title: Nsight Compute Profiling Guide — Roofline Charts
Exact_Page_Section_Table_Equation: Roofline Charts, §2.9.1 Overview; memory bandwidth boundary and memory-bound region
Evidence: NVIDIA's roofline guidance states that kernel performance depends on data-feed rate, memory bandwidth and memory traffic, and uses the achieved point to identify memory-bound versus compute-bound behavior.
Applicability: GPU profiling and roofline analysis where the relevant counters are available.
Limitations: Roofline classification depends on correct data-path/counter scope and does not capture every latency or control-divergence effect.

Rule_Name: Training Memory Traffic Must Be Evaluated as a Bandwidth Concern Separately From Training Capacity
Rule_Description: When training performance depends on movement of parameters, gradients, optimizer states, activations, or input data, evaluate the associated memory traffic/bandwidth rather than reusing capacity-feasibility rules alone.
Inputs: Training data movement; parameters; gradients; optimizer states; activations; measured bandwidth
Condition: Training memory traffic is materially involved in the target workload
Output_Decision: PERFORM TRAINING BANDWIDTH/LOCALITY ANALYSIS
Source_Title: Roofline: An Insightful Visual Performance Model for Multicore Architectures
Exact_Page_Section_Table_Equation: Roofline model; operational intensity and memory-traffic performance ceiling
Evidence: Roofline links performance limits to memory traffic and operational intensity, supporting separate performance analysis of memory movement rather than capacity alone.
Applicability: Training kernels or input pipelines where memory traffic materially affects execution.
Limitations: This rule does not estimate training traffic without workload-specific data.

Rule_Name: Inference Weight and Dynamic-State Traffic Must Be Evaluated Separately From Inference Capacity
Rule_Description: For inference, evaluate memory traffic caused by weight reads, KV-cache access, batching/concurrency, and runtime data movement when evidence indicates bandwidth may constrain serving performance.
Inputs: Weight traffic; KV-cache traffic; concurrency; achieved bandwidth; profiling
Condition: Inference workload shows material memory traffic or profiling evidence of memory limitation
Output_Decision: PERFORM INFERENCE BANDWIDTH/LOCALITY ANALYSIS
Source_Title: Nsight Compute Profiling Guide — Roofline Charts
Exact_Page_Section_Table_Equation: Roofline Charts, §2.9.1 Overview; memory traffic and achieved performance
Evidence: NVIDIA documents memory traffic as a determinant of GPU kernel performance and provides memory-bandwidth roofline analysis.
Applicability: GPU inference kernels where memory traffic can be measured or profiled.
Limitations: Does not establish a universal bytes-per-token or inference bandwidth requirement.

Rule_Name: Bandwidth Feasibility Should Compare Workload Demand With Validated Sustained/Applicable Bandwidth
Rule_Description: Use the existing DSS bandwidth-feasibility relationship only when required workload bandwidth and applicable sustained/validated bandwidth are both available and comparable in scope.
Inputs: BW_required; BW_available_sustained
Condition: Both workload demand and comparable sustained/validated available bandwidth are known
Output_Decision: USE CPU-P3-F02 AS THE EXISTING FEASIBILITY RELATIONSHIP
Source_Title: Optimizing Memory Bandwidth on Stream Triad
Exact_Page_Section_Table_Equation: STREAM measurement methodology; sustainable memory bandwidth
Evidence: Intel establishes STREAM as a method for measuring sustainable memory bandwidth; the DSS feasibility comparison uses measured/validated quantities rather than peak specifications.
Applicability: Bandwidth-constrained workload planning when comparable sustained bandwidth is available.
Limitations: The feasibility comparison is a DSS-derived gate; no universal safety margin is assumed.

Rule_Name: Theoretical-Only Bandwidth Must Produce Preliminary Evidence Rather Than a Definitive Workload Feasibility Claim
Rule_Description: If only theoretical bandwidth is available, do not treat a successful theoretical comparison as definitive workload feasibility. Mark the result preliminary and request measurement or validation when practical.
Inputs: BW_required; Memory_Bandwidth_GBps; bandwidth status
Condition: The available-bandwidth input is theoretical/peak and no validated sustained value exists
Output_Decision: RETURN PRELIMINARY / VALIDATION REQUIRED
Source_Title: Sustainable Memory Bandwidth in Current High Performance Computers
Exact_Page_Section_Table_Equation: Discussion of sustainable bandwidth and application-performance interpretation
Evidence: McCalpin emphasizes sustainable bandwidth as a meaningful application-performance measure and notes architectural complexity affecting achievable bandwidth.
Applicability: All DSS bandwidth-feasibility cases relying only on specification bandwidth.
Limitations: Historical source; principle is general, but exact performance values are not transferable.

Rule_Name: Missing Workload or Measurement Evidence Must Be Classified as INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE, Not as a Bandwidth Bottleneck
Rule_Description: Do not infer a memory-bandwidth bottleneck solely from workload type. If required traffic, achieved bandwidth, comparable benchmark evidence, or profiling data are unavailable, return an evidence-status result rather than infeasibility.
Inputs: Required bandwidth inputs; achieved bandwidth; profiling/benchmark evidence
Condition: Evidence required to establish bandwidth demand or bottleneck is missing
Output_Decision: RETURN INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE
Source_Title: Nsight Compute Profiling Guide — Roofline Charts
Exact_Page_Section_Table_Equation: Roofline Charts, §2.9.1 Overview; achieved measurements and limiting factors
Evidence: The profiling guide uses measured/derived roofline quantities to classify limiting factors and emphasizes validating the data path and counters.
Applicability: Any workload for which bandwidth limitation is being considered.
Limitations: Absence of evidence is not evidence of feasibility or infeasibility.

Rule_Name: Capacity Result Must Be Inherited From Part 1
Rule_Description: Use the Part 1 applicable-memory capacity result without recalculating capacity in Part 5.
Inputs: Part1_Capacity_Result; Required_Applicable_Memory; Applicable_Available_Memory
Condition: Part 1 reports PASS
Output_Decision: CAPACITY_PASS
Source_Title: Part 1 Memory Capacity
Exact_Page_Section_Table_Equation: Part 1 applicable-capacity feasibility comparison
